entry.evidence: questions specific to the present paper were as follows: (1) how does surface water carbonate chemistry respond to an upwelling event?

sequences.source_document: Publisher full text from XML (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: The authors take from the literature that CO2-enriched, N-deficient OMZ water upwelled off Peru raises surface CO2 and that phytoplankton uptake can damp outgassing.
steps.quote: surface water carbonate chemistry is influenced by upwelling of CO 2 -enriched OMZ water

steps.action: The authors pose two questions: how surface carbonate chemistry responds to upwelling, and how OMZ water with different chemical signatures modulates it.
steps.quote: (1) how does surface water carbonate chemistry respond to an upwelling event?

steps.action: The authors design a mesocosm experiment that simulates upwelling with OMZ water from two sites differing in nutrient content and N:P, and compare it with natural upwelling in the ambient water.
steps.quote: An upwelling event was simulated in the mesocosms by addition of OMZ waters collected from two different locations

steps.action: The authors take the surrounding Pacific water, with its natural upwelling events and the co-occurring rare 2017 coastal El Niño, as found conditions to observe alongside the mesocosms.
steps.quote: together with the influence of a rare coastal El Niño event (Garreaud, 2018)

steps.action: Eight KOSMOS mesocosms of the group's own earlier technical design are deployed off Callao; the design and the deployment details are cited to the authors' earlier papers.
steps.quote: The technical design of these seagoing mesocosms is described by Riebesell et al. (2013).

steps.action: The authors set the conditions: they add Low DIN water (Station 3, 70 m) to M2, M3, M6 and M7 and Very low DIN water (Station 1, 30 m) to M1, M4, M5 and M8 on days 11-12, and add brine on days 13 and 33 to keep a halocline.
steps.quote: During the night of 8 March (day 11), ∼ 10 m 3 of OMZ water was added to 14–17 m of each mesocosm.

steps.action: The authors sample the mesocosms and the Pacific at integrated depths daily or every second day over 50 d, measuring TA (titration), pHT (spectrophotometric), DIC (measured only to day 10 because of a malfunction), nutrients and CTD profiles (§2.4-§2.5).
steps.quote: Depth-integrated samples were taken from the surface (0–10 m for day 3–28) and bottom layer (10–17 m for day 3–28) of the mesocosms

steps.action: The authors infer pCO2, DIC and the calcite and aragonite saturation states from pHT and TA with CO2SYS (Lueker-refitted Mehrbach constants), propagate uncertainties with seacarb, and set up the Pacific air-sea flux FCO2 = k K0 ΔpCO2 from GLDAS wind (§2.6 ¶3-¶4).
steps.quote: were performed with the Excel version of CO2SYS (Version 2.1; Pierrot et al., 2006)

steps.action: The authors report the time series (§3.1-§3.2): DIN depletion after addition, chl a blooms, and a pCO2 rise above 900 µatm followed by a rapid drop; M3 (delayed) and M4 (persistently high pCO2) diverge; the Pacific shows lower pH, higher pCO2 and aragonite under-saturation at the bottom before day 13.
steps.quote: surface p CO 2 in the mesocosms decreased quickly and reached minima at 340–500 µ atm (except M3 and M4)

steps.action: The authors estimate the Pacific air-sea CO2 flux as constantly positive (4.2-14.0 mmol C m-2 d-1, correlated with wind, r2 = 0.4) and report propagated uncertainties per variable: saturation states 5.1 %, pCO2 3.8 %, DIC 0.3 % (§4.1 ¶1).
steps.quote: The air–sea CO 2 flux in the Pacific was constantly positive throughout our study

steps.action: The authors check the calculated DIC against the measured DIC for 53 pairs (days 3-10), find a mean residual of -8.27 µmol kg-1, and find no correlation of the residuals with pHT, TA or temperature.
steps.quote: The calculated DIC values were generally in agreement with the measured values ( r 2 = 0.985 ; p < 0.005 )

steps.action: The authors check instrument performance: triplicate pH precision (mean SD 0.0012), CRM control charts for TA (poor accuracy, 17.69 µmol kg-1 low, corrected by CRM calibration) and a range chart of duplicate CRMs (§4.1 ¶3-¶4).
steps.quote: 90.5 % of the measured TA values of CRM fell between warning limits

steps.action: The authors compare the post-addition mesocosm pCO2 with the ambient Pacific (>775 µatm) and with published 2013 observations for the area.
steps.quote: These values also agree with reported observations for our study area in 2013

steps.action: The authors set two rivals for the pCO2 decline: outgassing, possibly enhanced by El Niño warming, against biological uptake.
steps.quote: The declining p CO 2 could be partially attributed by CO 2 outgassing

steps.action: The authors exclude gas exchange as the sole cause, because outgassing cannot produce CO2 under-saturation relative to the atmosphere.
steps.quote: However, air–sea gas exchange could not explain surface CO 2 under-saturation in relation to the atmosphere

steps.action: The authors use M4, the mesocosm with little biomass buildup, as an internal reference: its DIC stayed high.
steps.quote: This interpretation is supported by the continuously high DIC in M4 where photosynthetic biomass buildup was substantially lower

steps.action: The authors keep biological uptake as the primary driver of the DIC loss, while stating that gas exchange in the mesocosms was not measured (no N2O, to protect the 15N incubations) and that no C budget was possible.
steps.quote: the loss of DIC (except M4) was primarily driven by biological uptake and phytoplankton growth

steps.action: The authors compare the treatments: DIC drawdown in Low DIN was 41.0 µmol kg-1 higher than in Very low DIN, days 13-24, excluding M3 and M4 (Mann-Whitney p = 0.05), matching the expectation for added limiting nutrient.
steps.quote: the uptake of DIC was higher in the Low DIN mesocosms, which received more input of DIN from OMZ water addition

steps.action: Because the DIC difference was not reflected in POC, the authors invoke an auxiliary instead: biomass was retained by A. sanguinea and C was channeled to DOC, supported by co-authors' DOC data (Igarza et al.).
steps.quote: much of the consumed DIC could have been channeled to the dissolved organic carbon (DOC) pool

steps.action: The authors propose mesocosm-specific phytoplankton succession (diatoms to A. sanguinea, absent in M3 and M4) to explain the post-day-24 divergence.
steps.quote: One factor that may have controlled the differences in CO 2 increase are the mesocosm-specific phytoplankton succession patterns.

steps.action: The authors match the pCO2 timing in M3 (one-week delay) and M4 (persistently high) against the chl a buildup and the A. sanguinea occurrence.
steps.quote: the reduction in p CO 2 in M3 experienced a 1-week delay, which is consistent with the delayed buildup of chl a biomass

steps.action: The authors keep A. sanguinea as a key driver of the carbonate chemistry trend.
steps.quote: This strongly suggests that A. sanguinea was a key factor driving the trend of carbonate chemistry in the mesocosms.

steps.action: The authors attribute the late surface bloom and pCO2 decline to nutrient input from Inca tern excrement.
steps.quote: This bloom was likely fueled by surface eutrophication due to defecating sea birds.

steps.action: The authors reject a direct acidifying effect of the acidic droppings, because alkalinity did not decrease.
steps.quote: However, this should have been visible in decreasing alkalinity, which was not the case.

steps.action: The authors defend the mesocosm auxiliaries (brine effects, enclosure gas exchange, mixing) with others' studies, and concede that there were no control mesocosms.
steps.quote: the effects of the brine on the enclosed organisms have been discussed in past studies and considered negligible for a salinity increase

steps.action: The authors compare the Pacific fluxes with Takahashi et al. (2009), the Paulmier et al. (2008) high-flux criterion, and Friederich et al. (2008), which averaged 0-200 km offshore and reported lower values.
steps.quote: These results of air–sea CO 2 fluxes were slightly higher than observations by Friederich et al. (2008) along the coast of Peru

steps.action: In a back-of-envelope comparison, upper-bound outgassing over 10 d (0.142 mol m-2) is set against the mesocosm DIC drawdown (1.18-1.60 mol m-2).
steps.quote: This shows that biological processes drawing down CO 2 are stronger than loss by air–sea gas exchange.

steps.action: The authors weigh the El Niño influence against reports of reduced fluxes during El Niño (Feely et al. 1999, 2002) and conclude that its local magnitude cannot be determined.
steps.quote: it is difficult to conclude the magnitude of the coastal El Niño influence on the local CO 2 fluxes in our study

steps.action: The authors keep the observation of aragonite under-saturation in the Pacific subsurface and in the OMZ source waters as a potential dissolution risk for calcifiers.
steps.quote: our observations of aragonite under-saturation in the Pacific suggest a potential risk of dissolution for marine calcifiers

steps.action: The authors conclude that the site was a strong CO2 source, but that biological drawdown can quickly turn it into a sink; the El Niño influence remains unclear.
steps.quote: evidence from our mesocosm experiment suggests biological responses that draw down DIC can quickly turn a CO 2 source into a sink

sequences.source_document: Open discussion of preprint bg-2021-111 (RC1, RC2, AC2 with supplement AC2-S)

steps.action: Referee 2 (RC2 ¶2, ¶6) asked about complications from the brine addition and the mesocosm setup; the authors added a discussion of brine effects and enclosure gas exchange, conceding that a brine effect cannot be fully excluded.
steps.quote: we acknowledge that an effect cannot fully be excluded for the Peru study and will disclose that in the revised version of the manuscript

steps.action: Referee 2 (RC2 ¶2) asked for other approaches to separate gas exchange from biological uptake; the authors added why N2O gas-exchange tracing was not used.
steps.quote: However, this was not carried out in our study because it may interfere with 15N label incubations (Schulz et al., 2021).

steps.action: The authors declined to add a dissolved-oxygen analysis to separate biological from gas-exchange losses (RC2 ¶2, ¶10), citing scope and other papers.
steps.quote: However, this would be outside the scope of this paper

steps.action: The authors revised background wording on N removal (RC2 ¶4) and on anthropogenic CO2 uptake (RC2 ¶5); the published sentence drops 'uptake'.
steps.quote: We changed “nitrogen” to “biologically available nitrogen”.

steps.action: The authors answered the question about the temperature of the added water (RC2 ¶6) by arguing that the in situ mesocosms followed the ambient temperature, with no new work.
steps.quote: the mesocosms were in a way temperature controlled as they represented the real-world temperature profile in the upwelling areas

steps.action: The authors answered the carbon-budget request (RC2 ¶8) by explaining that no reasonable budget was possible, and added that explanation to the text without a new analysis.
steps.quote: With a lack of estimation of CO2 gas exchange, this approach was unsuccessful to calculate a reasonable C budget in this study.

steps.action: Referee 2 (RC2 ¶9) linked the lack of POC buildup to the halocline; the authors clarified the point and added the A. sanguinea retention explanation.
steps.quote: brine addition is unlikely the reason for the absence of POC buildup in M4

steps.action: Referee 2 (RC2 ¶11) asked whether bird droppings affected pH; the authors added the acidity argument. The published version rejects the effect via the unchanged alkalinity, whereas the rebuttal invoked counteracting productivity.
steps.quote: Therefore, the droppings may lower the pH of the surface water.

steps.action: Referee 2 (RC2 ¶12) asked whether hydrodynamics, rather than nutrients, drove the ecosystem change; the authors added the missing-control limitation and the Striebel et al. (2013) mixing study.
steps.quote: It would be ideal to have control mesocosms that were treated the same way except the OMZ water addition

Describe the response and its modulation by OMZ water signature
Outgassing vs biological uptake; succession; seabird nutrient input
Under-saturation impossible by outgassing; M4 without bloom keeps high DIC

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Natural upwelling events recur in the Pacific; El Niño is a single event
Measurement and calculation checks only; no control mesocosms
Biological uptake kept as best explanation; El Niño effect unresolved
Two referees; text additions, no new analysis

end.claim: Simulated upwelling acidified mesocosm surface water (pHT lowered by 0.1-0.2, pCO2 above 900 µatm); pCO2 then fell to near or below atmospheric level mainly through phytoplankton uptake, with A. sanguinea dominance and seabird excrement shaping later dynamics, while the surrounding Pacific outgassed 4.2-14.0 mmol C m-2 d-1.

decisive_move.sentence: Setting the upwelling conditions by adding two OMZ water masses to the eight mesocosms produced the perturbation whose drawdown carries every mesocosm claim.

gates.evidence: Action: the treatment design (two DIN levels) was chosen to test upwelling effects, but this paper states questions, not hypotheses (§1 ¶4). Claim: the biological-drawdown claim faced the outgassing rival via under-saturation, the M4 contrast and a flux-versus-drawdown budget (§4.2 ¶2, §4.3 ¶1), but there were no control mesocosms (§4.2 ¶5). Registration: only the experimental design and additions were fixed before the data; the analyses and rivals appear post hoc.

imports.item: Control charts and range charts with warning and control limits for CRM measurements
Mann–Whitney U test for treatment differences
Spectrophotometric pH with m-cresol purple indicator dye and dye-addition correction
Infrared absorption DIC analysis (LI-COR LI-7000 on AIRICA)
Composition and acidity of seabird excrement (uric acid, ammonium, N and P content)

novelty_claims.quote: [...] insights into how inorganic C cycling links to chemical signatures of OMZ waters in a natural plankton community
our observations can serve as the first evidence of carbonate chemistry dynamics in the coastal Peruvian upwelling system during a coastal El Niño event
hence provided unique insights into the CO 2 dynamics during a rare coastal El Niño event
As a unique dataset that characterized nearshore carbonate chemistry with a high temporal resolution during a rare coastal El Niño event

limits: Composition none_fits: the walk is a set-condition field mesocosm experiment monitored descriptively, with found Pacific conditions alongside. Rival explanations (outgassing vs uptake, succession, seabird input) are weighed after the fact, with no crucial test shared by all rivals; this is neither strong inference nor a pure trace series. Sub-claims and statuses: the Pacific air-sea flux of 4.2-14.0 mmol C m-2 d-1 is estimate_with_resolution, although wind-based k uncertainty is not propagated (inference). The treatment effect on DIC drawdown (p = 0.05, M3 and M4 excluded) is a weak best_explanation. A. sanguinea as key driver is best_explanation, resting on community data from the co-authors' overview paper (Bach et al. 2020a), not shown here. Seabird fertilization of the second bloom is best_explanation, based on reported tern presence and cited DON data. Aragonite under-saturation in the Pacific subsurface is ambiguous within the 5.1 % propagated uncertainty. The El Niño influence on local fluxes is explicitly unresolved (no conclusion). Process the document does not show: there were no control mesocosms without OMZ addition. Gas exchange inside the mesocosms was neither measured nor computed, so the uptake/outgassing split is not quantified. DIC was measured only to day 10, so later DIC values are calculated with a known -8.27 µmol kg-1 bias. TA accuracy was poor (17.69 µmol kg-1 offset) and was corrected by CRM calibration. Treatment replication (n = 4) is reduced when M3 and M4 are excluded post hoc. Neither the review record nor the paper states whether any analysis was planned in advance (inference: none was).

disagreements.target: Friederich et al. (2008), air-sea CO2 fluxes along the Peruvian coast
disagreements.support: The nearshore fluxes measured here are higher; the authors attribute the difference to Friederich et al. averaging 0-200 km offshore, where pCO2 is lower.
disagreements.quote: These results of air–sea CO 2 fluxes were slightly higher than observations by Friederich et al. (2008) along the coast of Peru

disagreements.target: General expectation that adding a limiting nutrient enhances biomass buildup
disagreements.support: Higher DIC drawdown in Low DIN mesocosms was not matched by more POC, which the authors explain by biomass retention and DOC channeling.
disagreements.quote: Such differences in DIC uptake, however, were not reflected in the buildup of particulate organic carbon (POC) in the mesocosms

alternatives_considered.chosen: Measured pHT and TA as the input pair for carbonate system calculations
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Measured DIC as an input (available only for days 3-10)
alternatives_considered.reason: Malfunction of the AIRICA DIC system after day 10

alternatives_considered.chosen: pHT standard uncertainty of 0.01 in uncertainty propagation
alternatives_considered.reason: The repeatability SD covers only random error; no CRMs exist to correct systematic pH error

alternatives_considered.chosen: Propagating only pHT and TA uncertainties
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Including uncertainties in nutrients, salinity and temperature
alternatives_considered.reason: Their contributions are often small (<0.1 %; Orr et al., 2018)

alternatives_considered.chosen: No gas-exchange tracer in the mesocosms
alternatives_considered.alternatives: N2O addition to monitor air-sea gas exchange
alternatives_considered.reason: It would have interfered with 15N label incubations

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Carbon budget to separate outgassing from biological uptake
alternatives_considered.reason: High DOC variability, unconstrained gas exchange, and a water column not homogeneously mixed

alternatives_considered.chosen: All eight mesocosms receiving OMZ water (two treatments of four)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Control mesocosms treated the same way except for OMZ water addition
alternatives_considered.reason: To ensure enough replicates despite the cost of mesocosm experimentation
